title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
summary: The core drills: ṭa–ka tonguing and tapping each finger a hundred times; how air vibrates in a bānsurī; three kinds of blowing and ten qualities of a good blow, first practised at a fire; fingering six and nine holes; bānsurī sizes; mūrchanā and ascent–descent in rhythm; then varṇas, sparśa and mīṇḍ.

blocks.text: Practice of the tongue

It is proven by experience that touching the jihvā (tongue) in turn to the throat, the palate, the roof of the mouth and the teeth produces the sounds (ka), (ca), (ṭa) and (ta). In the same way, keep blowing into the bānsurī while saying ṭa and ka quickly and without a break, many times over. Just as the dir dir of the sitar turns one note into equal pieces, so [this] will make the sound coming out of the bānsurī beautiful with equal strokes. If at first some fault is heard in the breath because of this action, do not be put off by it; keep practising for a long time, with confidence, like this: (ṭa ka ṭa ka ṭa ka). Once it is mastered, it will become beautiful. These same two syllables will turn Sa into Sa Sa Sa Sa and Re into Re Re Re Re.
If, instead of ṭa-ka, one relies on some other syllable such as ca or ta, the practitioner will regret it later, because along with the breath the saliva must also be kept in check.
Practice of the fingers

It is true that the fingers gain strength from repeatedly and quickly gripping something and letting it go; this natural exercise goes on anyway in various tasks such as washing clothes. But because in these tasks there is no devotion to the exercise, or absorption in it, we do not give it the place of sādhanā (practice). So, with the fingers held straight on a table and without moving the hand, keep striking with just one finger, with full strength, a hundred times in a row, counting; then strike with the second, third and fourth finger in the same way. Then close the holes on the bānsurī and, in the same way, keep striking each finger quickly on the hole of the bānsurī until pain arises at the root of the finger. Then strike two fingers together, and then three fingers together. By doing this every day without a break, the speed of the fingers will keep increasing month by month, and this will give you good help in the svara practice that comes later. Then, if you also want to learn another instrument, such as the tabla, you will progress quickly in that too. The following śloka points to these very things.

blocks.verse:
तन्तु वाद्ये भवेत्कम्पः नेत्राभ्याम् स विलोक्यते।
वायु वाद्ये तु यः कम्पः सोऽनुमानेन बुध्यते।६३।
blocks.text: In a tantu vādya (stringed instrument) there is kampa (vibration), and it is seen with the eyes; but the vibration in a vāyu vādya (wind instrument) is understood by inference.

That is, in instruments such as the vīṇā and the sitar the string is made to vibrate by the hand, so we can see that kampana (vibration) with our eyes. But the bānsurī is a vāyu vādya (wind instrument): the air from the mouth sets up vibration in the air inside the bānsurī, so we can establish that vibration only by reasoning (anumāna, inference). For it is a scientific truth that nāda (musical sound) cannot arise without vibration. Only a thing that has lacāva (elasticity) can vibrate. A string has elasticity, so it vibrates. Air too has elasticity, so it vibrates. But the vibration of a string differs from the vibration of air in direction. If the string's vibration is across its width, the air's vibration is along its length. The string's length is tied to the pegs and is tightened, but the air's width is bound and held tight by the bamboo. So if the bamboo cracks for some reason, the air is no longer held tight and no sound is produced. Like air, water too is elastic, so the jal taraṅg is a successful instrument. But water cannot vibrate without the support of air, and in the same way a string does not vibrate without the support of air. So for vibration the support of air has to be taken. In the bānsurī, air is made to vibrate by air, in air. In stringed instruments, material is made to vibrate by material, in air. In instruments such as the shehnai, material is made to vibrate by air, in air. In covered instruments (such as the mṛdaṅga), skin is made to vibrate by the hands, in air. The saying (jātaḥ prāṇāgni saṃyogāt) [it is born from the union of breath and fire] is a scientific truth.

blocks.verse:
प्रवाहितोऽल्प बद्धश्च मुक्तश्चेति त्रिधानिलाः।
बंशादि निर्मिते वाद्ये नादस्योत्पत्तिहेतवः।६४।
blocks.text: Pravāhita (flowing), alpabaddha (slightly confined) and mukta (free): air is of these three kinds, and these are the causes of the production of sound in an instrument made of bamboo and the like.

Whatever metal the bānsurī may be made of, the nāda (musical sound) in it arises only from air. Here air is of three kinds. The first is pravāhita (flowing): the air that flows from the player's mouth as breath through a very narrow passage and is confined on all sides. The second is (alpabaddha, slightly confined): the air that fills the inside of the bānsurī. And the third is (mukta, free): the air through which the sound is able to reach the listeners' ears. Seen this way, living beings too fall into these same three classes: 1 animals, 2 humans, 3 gods. But to see the whole world as a bānsurī, I would have to reach the level of a bānsurī player. Now we write the features and kinds of the most confined air.

blocks.verse:
मुखतो वायु निर्धातः फूत्कार इति कथ्यते।
प्राकृतो वैकृतश्चैव कृत्रिमस्तु तृतीयकः।६५।
blocks.text: The issuing of air from the mouth is called phūtkāra (blowing). It is prākṛta (natural) and vaikṛta (cultivated), and the third is kṛtrima (artificial).

That is, the directed issue, that is, the flow, of air from the mouth is called phūtkāra, that is, phūṅk (blowing). It has three kinds: prākṛta (natural), vaikṛta (cultivated) and kṛtrima (artificial). The Tripurā bānsurī is played with natural blowing, the āḍī (transverse) bānsurī with cultivated blowing, and the bānsurī with a jibbhī (fipple) with artificial blowing. For natural blowing no mukharandhra (mouth-hole) of any kind has to be made in the bānsurī; the sound is made by the player's skill alone. For cultivated blowing a mouth-hole and a cork have to be provided, and the player makes [the breath] fit for sound with some effort. For artificial blowing the bānsurī maker has to make all the effort, and the player gets the sound out easily. Man follows the middle path, so for him cultivated blowing is the best.

blocks.verse:
फूत्कारों वैकृतः श्रेष्ठः प्राकृतो मध्यम स्मृतः।
जड़ाश्रितस्तु फूत्कारो दोष यक्तोऽधमो भवेत्।६६।
blocks.text: Cultivated blowing is the best; natural blowing is held to be middling; blowing that relies on an inert device is faulty and is the lowest.

Whatever the kind of blowing, the cause of nādotpatti (the production of sound) in the bānsurī is only the friction of air. When moving air strikes, many kinds of vibration begin in the still air. Differences in the fixed width and length of the air bring rise and fall in the sound. This very rise and fall is given the name sargam (the scale of notes). The following śloka says just this.

blocks.verse:
मुखरन्ध्रे विनिक्षिप्तः फूत्कारो घर्षको भवेत्।
तेन घृष्टोऽचलो वायुस्तेन नादः प्रजायते।६७।
blocks.text: Sent into the mukharandhra (mouth-hole), the phūtkāra (breath) becomes the rubbing [agent]; the still air, rubbed by it, gives rise to nāda (musical sound).

So, for sound to arise in any bānsurī, the rubbing air, that is, the phūṅk (breath), must be slanting. If the flow of the rubbing [air] becomes strong, the vibration of the air begins to increase in the order of twofold, threefold and fourfold. This action cannot be seen with the eyes, but as a result of these actions the ears hear in the sounds the difference Sa Ṡa Ṗa Ṡa. So we infer that in the enclosed air inside the bānsurī the capacity to vibrate takes many forms, depending on the length of the bānsurī. So with slackness or strength in the flow of the breath, the capacity changes at once. Now, leaving this subtlety to the scientists, I must move on to the elements that concern the practice of music. So, about the qualities of the breath in the bānsurī —

blocks.verse:
सौम्याकृतिः, प्रलम्बासुः समदृष्टिः, सुनादकृत्।
नातिवक्र, शिरः कायो, मन्द्रतार नियन्त्रितः।६८।
blocks.text: Calm in appearance, long-breathed, with a steady gaze, making a good sound; with head and body not too bent; controlled in the low and high registers;

blocks.verse:
सीतकार रहितः, सूक्ष्मों, मुखरन्ध्र वशीकृतः।
सुकम्पितश्च फूप्कारो ज्ञेयो दशगुणान्वितः।६९।
blocks.text: free of hissing, fine, held under control at the mukharandhra (mouth-hole), and well vibrated: blowing should be known to have these ten qualities.

The breath for the bānsurī has the ten qualities above, and opposite to them there can be as many faults. The practitioner has to avoid the faults and move towards the qualities; those qualities are explained here. — (1) While blowing, the face should be pleasant and calm. (2) The breath should come out for a long time. (3) The gaze should be steady and the eyes open naturally. (4) There should be sweetness in the breath. (5) The body should not be too bent. (6) The breath should be so controlled that the notes of the mandra (low), madhya (middle) and tāra (high) saptaka (octave) can be produced at will. (7) The face should not be distorted while blowing. (8) No kind of hissing should be heard with the breath, or before or after it. (9) The stream of the breath should be so thin that it can produce sound even in small holes. (10) There should be a regular vibration in the breath that is heard like a wave. — All these qualities are for the āḍī (transverse) and the Tripurā bānsurī.

For the bānsurī with a jībh (fipple) the following points should be kept in mind. (1) Do not take the bānsurī far into the mouth; as far as possible, keep it at the front edge of the lips. (2) Tighten the breath in proportion to the room there is in the jibbhī (fipple) built inside the bānsurī, so that there is control over the sounds of two octaves. (3) Saliva should not come along with the breath. — The above qualities and faults should be watched closely in the early period. Some people even make use of a mirror.

If one listens carefully to the sound of one's own breath, an irregular vibration will be seen in the sound, like the flickering flame of a lamp. Taking that as a fault, several actions for regular vibration are described in the following śloka.

blocks.verse:
हृत्कम्पःकण्ठः कम्पश्च जिह्वा मूलस्य कम्पनम्।
तथैवाधर कम्पश्च कराग्रौ कम्पितौ क्वचित्।७०।
blocks.text: Vibration of the heart, vibration of the throat, vibration of the root of the tongue, and likewise vibration of the adhara (lips); and sometimes the fingertips are made to vibrate.

That is, the vibration that comes from an exercise like the way a dog keeps panting in the hot season is called hṛtkampa, that is, heart vibration. For the bānsurī this is the best vibration. Some people make the vibration with the throat — that is middling. And some people make the lips or the hands vibrate — this is the lowest. The practitioner should practise the best kind of breath close to a guru (teacher), for otherwise one does not see one's own faults. To blow into the Tripurā bānsurī, one should close the open end of the bamboo from three sides and blow slantwise from one side; it is mainly because the breath is connected with three sides that it is named Tripurā. This is what the following śloka says.

blocks.verse:
भागत्रयम् प्रपूयैंर्व फूतकारो यत्र साध्यते।
अतस्ताम् त्रिपुराम् बंशीम् कथयन्ति मनीषिणः।७१।
blocks.text: Where the blowing is accomplished by covering three parts [of the opening], the wise therefore call that bānsurī the Tripurā.
Some practitioners blow the bānsurī two or four times, fail, and lose heart; so an effort is being made to awaken their enthusiasm again.

blocks.verse:
वाद्यम् विहाय फूत्कारम् पावकादौ न्यसेत्पुरा।
तत्र सिध्दम् हि फूत्कारम् वाद्ये सभ्यक् प्रसाधयेत्।७२।
blocks.text: Leaving the instrument aside, one should first direct the breath at fire and the like; then the breath perfected there should be properly applied to the instrument.

That is, a new practitioner should first practise blowing at a fire; when the practice of blowing at a fire has been mastered over a week, then one should try for sound in the bānsurī with that breath. For when the lips are not balanced, the flow of the breath becomes crooked, and when too much air comes out in the breath, the breath does not last. So, to make the stream of the breath long, thin and straight, it will be right, on spiritual, scientific and Vedic evidence, to regard Agni deva (the god of fire) himself as the very first guru (teacher). Śrī Manu, the author of the dharmaśāstra, has also given fire the place of guru: (gururagnirdvijātīnām) [fire is the guru of the twice-born]; (tamaso mā jyotirgamaya) [lead me from darkness to light]. All these sayings create faith in fire in us, and through faith both skill and knowledge become easy to gain. In this way, by trying many times, the breath is mastered and begins to produce a beautiful sound in the bānsurī in a balanced way. If the flow of the breath is joined to the mukharandhra (mouth-hole) on the bānsurī, there can be three kinds of it, of which only the third kind is correct; the other two kinds are incorrect. Look at the figure below and try.
The flow of the breath keeps spreading out like light —
I hope these figures will be of proper benefit to practitioners.

blocks.verse:
जिह्वावतींम् सुजिह्वां तु मुखाग्रेण निनादयेत्।
मध्यतार परीक्षाया मुत्तीर्णाम् सरस, स्वराम्।७३।
blocks.text: The Jihvāvatī (duct bānsurī) with a good jihvā (fipple) should be sounded with the front of the mouth; [it should be one] that has passed the test of the middle and high [registers] and has sweet notes.

In the āḍī (transverse) bānsurī or the Tripurā bānsurī the sweetness of the breath depends on the practitioner, but in the Jihvāvatī (duct bānsurī) the sweetness of the breath depends mostly on the maker, and making it is somewhat difficult. So it will be best, for the most part, to buy a bānsurī with a jībh (fipple) from the market, because that maker's hand is practised in making it. Even so, the faults that are possible should be tested for at the time of buying. If there is no hissing in the breath and all seven notes come out properly in both octaves, it will be right to buy such a bānsurī from the market and play it. While playing, only the front part of the mouth should touch it; and, avoiding again and again faults of posture such as puffing the cheeks and shutting the eyes, one should practise on the notes of both octaves with the help of 'ṭa' or 'ka' on the tongue. Now some light is thrown on the rakhāva (placement) of the fingers.

blocks.verse:
दक्षिणांगुलिभि स्तृाणि तृीणि बामांगुलीयकैः।
प्राच्छादनं तु छिद्राणाम् षट् स्वरायाम् प्रकल्पितम्।७४।
blocks.text: Three [holes] with the fingers of the right [hand], three with the fingers of the left: this is the covering of the holes laid down for the ṣaṭsvarā (six-note bānsurī).

That is, if the bānsurī has six holes, the three upper holes should be closed with three fingers of the right hand, and the three lower holes with three fingers of the left hand. Keep in mind that the fingers should be as straight as possible, because if they are bent, success in practising the komal notes will later be hard to achieve. If the middle part of the middle finger is on the hole, the other two fingers will straighten by themselves. But if the bānsurī is large, the fingers have to be slanted somewhat because of the distance between the holes. Even then, no finger should be raised in the middle and bent at the tip. It will be better if this too is done under a guru's guidance. Otherwise many kinds of faults and doubts will unsettle the practitioner. Now the placement of the fingers on nine holes is described.

blocks.verse:
तूर्याष्टमौ कनिष्ठाभ्याम् वादकाश्छादयन्त्यथ।
विपरीतस्थितेडङ्गुष्ठां छिद्रे रक्षन्ति साधकाः।७५।
blocks.text: Then players cover the fourth and the eighth [holes] with the little fingers; and practitioners keep the thumb on the hole placed on the opposite side.

blocks.verse:
पूर्वक्रमेण छिद्राणि तर्जन्याद्यंगुलीयकैंः।
प्राच्छादयेदवक्रेण स्वल्प वक्रेण वा क्वचित्।७६।
blocks.text: The holes should be covered in the earlier order with the fingers beginning with the index finger, keeping them straight, or sometimes slightly bent.

That is, closing the holes in order from the top with the index and the other fingers according to the earlier rule, in a bānsurī with eight holes close the fourth and the eighth holes with the kaniṣṭhā, that is, the smallest fingers. If, besides the eight, there is a ninth hole from the bottom on the opposite side, close it with the thumb. If, when making the bānsurī, the holes are made with the placement of the fingers in mind, the holes will not all lie in a straight line but will certainly look somewhat crooked; but this brings quick success in practice and does no harm. If, tempted by good looks, the holes are set in a straight line, crookedness will come into the placement of the fingers, and that could stand in the way of success. That is why practitioners today feel hardship on large bānsurīs. It was largely to solve these very difficulties that the late Śrī Pannalal Ghosh ji had his fingers lengthened by surgery. This was certainly a sign of his boundless devotion, but for his followers it became a hard nut to crack.

The solution I have found for this will be scientifically acceptable to all. If a separate hole is made between Dha and Ni for komal Ni, and between Re and Ga for komal Ga, there are three benefits: (1) the distance between the holes becomes smaller; (2) clarity comes easily in rāgas with komal notes; (3) greater success is gained in the action of mīṇḍ (glide). So practitioners are requested to make and practise on a nine-hole bānsurī from the very beginning. This is made clear in the figure ahead. Here figure (7) is for those who like to keep the left hand below. Figure (8) is for those with the opposite preference. We have made this design after checking carefully that it poses no difficulty for the placement of human fingers. Here the hole at the very top is for placing the thumb, so by giving it a place on the edge of the bānsurī it is shown that the thumb too is placed not fully at the back but pressed to the right or the left. If you feel some discomfort, you can make the rows of holes more crooked or straighter, depending on the thickness of the bānsurī. This will make no difference to the notes, because the difference between the notes depends on the distance between the holes and on the size of the holes.

At the start, practitioners should practise on a bānsurī one hasta (cubit) long, measured by their own arm. Then after one year it will be right to practise on one of one and a half hastas, and after two years on a bānsurī of about two hastas. This process will lead the placement of the fingers naturally towards progress. See the length of the bānsurī, according to the tastes of the three stages of life — childhood, youth and maturity — in the ślokas written below.

blocks.verse:
बालानाम् तु रुचि स्तारे युवानाम् मध्य सप्तके।
प्रौणानाम् वादकानाम् तु रुचिर्मन्द्रे प्रजायते।७७।
blocks.text: Children take delight in the high register, the young in the middle octave; and in mature players the delight arises in the low [register].
That is, children like a bānsurī of the tāra (high) octave, young people one of the madhya (middle) octave, and mature people one of the mandra (low) octave.

blocks.verse:
हस्तार्ध परिमिता तारी मध्या हस्तैक मानका।
सार्धहस्ता भवेन्मन्द्रा द्विहस्ताऽपि क्वचित।७८।
blocks.text: The Tārī (small, high-pitched bānsurī) measures half a hasta (cubit), the Madhyā (medium bānsurī) one hasta; the Mandrā (large, low-pitched bānsurī) should be one and a half hastas, and sometimes even two hastas.

It is a proof of the Supreme Lord's wondrous glory that whatever is good for a creature is also what it likes. So animals and birds give up food when they are sick. So in childhood there is a natural liking for the Tārī bānsurī (of the high octave), and in youth for the Madhyā bānsurī (of the middle octave). This too is a special feature of the bānsurī. If the placement of the fingers is to be kept up, it will be best to practise on a small bānsurī from childhood. In the above śloka the dimensions of all three bānsurīs are given. The Tārī bānsurī is half a hasta (cubit) long, the Madhyā one hasta long and the Mandra one and a half hastas long. Here and there, practitioners with long fingers even play a bānsurī two hastas long.

blocks.verse:
अंगुल्यपान्त भागेन छिद्राच्छादः प्रसंशितः।
नात्यग्रेण न मूलेन बंशी छिद्रान् प्रपेरयेत्।७९।
blocks.text: Covering the holes with the part of the finger just short of its end is praised; one should not press on the bānsurī's holes with the very tip or with the base [of the finger].

blocks.verse:
ऋजुस्वराणामुच्वारे क्लिष्ताम् परिकल्पयन्।
श्रुतिस्पर्शधिया चैव स्थापये दंगुलीयकान्।८०।
blocks.text: Foreseeing difficulty in sounding the ṛju (plain) notes, and with a mind to touching the śrutis, one should place the fingers [accordingly].

The practitioner should bear in mind that sometimes, to sound komal notes, even half a hole will have to be opened, and then it may be impossible to bend the finger. The second point is that if, in going from one note to another, touching the śrutis in between — that is, mīṇḍ (glide) — is wanted, then the placement of the fingers can be a hindrance. So, to be saved from troubles that will come in the future, place the fingers correctly right now. For this it is best to set the upāntya (next-to-last) part of the fingers on the holes. Some people bend the long finger for the convenience of the little finger. This is wholly harmful. For clarity, look at the figures.

blocks.verse:
शतम् शतम् समाहन्या दंगुलीयान् पृथक् पृथक्।
अंग पीड़ाम् प्रसहयैव ह्यंग शक्तिः प्रवर्धते।८१।
blocks.text: One should strike the fingers a hundred times each, one by one; by enduring pain in the limb, the strength of the limb grows.

In this age of short lives, a special kind of practice for quick success is described in this śloka. Once the placement of the fingers on the bānsurī is well established, each finger should be struck in its place, separately, a hundred times each, so that with unbroken practice pain begins in the finger; and by keeping even the aching finger moving, strength will come quickly to the fingers, just as heating iron quickly makes it pliable. At the same time the mind, busy with counting, also gains concentration. If the fingers of both hands are struck one at a time, by turns, progress can be even faster. In the same way, it will be fitting first to cook the breath, the tongue and the fingers separately for a while, as described above — like rice, dal and vegetables — in the fire of practice with the water of faith added, and then to combine all three and move on to the practice of svara (notes) and laya (tempo). On this, see the śloka —

blocks.verse:
छिद्रान् सर्वान् समाच्छाद्य फूत्कारस्तु शनैः शनैः।
क्रीयते तेन यो नादो जायते प्रथमो हि सः।८२।
blocks.text: With all the holes covered, the blowing is done very gently; the sound that arises from it is indeed the first.

With all the holes in the bānsurī, however many there are, properly closed, the nāda (sound) that comes from blowing very gently — take that as the first note of the bānsurī. Keep in mind that if the holes are not completely closed, the note may change and become the eighth note.

blocks.verse:
अनामिकाम् समुत्थाय द्वितीयो नाद उच्यते।
मध्यमाम् तु समुत्थाप्य तृतीयो नाद्यते खलु।८३।
blocks.text: By lifting the ring finger the second sound is said [to arise]; by lifting the middle finger the third is indeed sounded.
That is, opening the lowest hole produces the second sound, and opening the second hole the third.

blocks.verse:
तर्जनीं च समुत्थाप्य तूर्यो नादो निनाद्यते।
अथानामिकामन्या मुत्थाप्यैव च पंचमः।८४।
blocks.text: By lifting the index finger the fourth sound is sounded; then, by lifting the other ring finger, the fifth.

That is, lifting the anāmikā, that is, the third finger, of the other hand produces the pañcama (fifth) note. But keep in mind that, as soon as that finger is lifted, the ring finger of the first hand, which was already raised, should be put back on its own hole. Otherwise, once all the fingers are lifted, the bānsurī will have no support and may fall to the ground.

blocks.verse:
मध्यमांश्च समुत्थाप्य नादः षष्ठ उदीयते।
समुत्थाप्य ततः सर्वान् प्रथमा नामिकाम् विना।८५।
blocks.text: By lifting the middle fingers the sixth sound arises. Then, by lifting all of them except the first ring finger,

blocks.verse:
प्राणाधातस्य वेगेन नाद्यते सप्तमः स्वरः।
ततः सर्वान् समाच्छाद्य तार निनाद्यते।८६।
blocks.text: with the force of the stroke of breath the seventh note is sounded. Then, covering all [the holes], the tāra (upper) [Sa] is sounded.

In the same order, lifting the next finger, that is, the middle finger, produces the sixth sound, that is, dhaivata (Dha), and lifting the last, the index finger, produces the seventh sound, called niṣāda (Ni). But the force of the breath, rising step by step, becomes so great by Ni that if, blowing with that same force, we close all the holes at once, the eighth sound, that is, Ṡa of the tāra (upper) octave, is produced.

blocks.verse:
तिव्राधातेन प्राणस्य क्रमसः पूर्व वद्यदा।
सप्तानाम् नादनम् कुर्यात् तदा नादा श्चतुर्दश।८७।
blocks.text: When, with a strong stroke of breath, one sounds the seven in order as before, then there are fourteen sounds.

If in this way one keeps lifting the fingers as before while increasing the strength of the breath, the seven notes of the second octave will be produced. So it is proved that by increasing the force of the breath the same seven sounds have gone into another octave — just as any number, on gaining a zero, changes from units to tens. But by blowing harder still, only two or three notes of the third octave can come out. In this way, in a bānsurī with six holes, usually a total of 15 śuddha (natural) notes are produced, in this order: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni | Ṡa Ṙe Ġa Ṁa Ṗa Ḋha Ṅi | Ṡa. For the remaining komal notes, the method of opening less than half a hole has to be adopted. In a bānsurī with eight holes there are holes for komal Ga and komal Dha as well.

blocks.verse:
सरी गमौ पधौ निश्चेत्येते सप्तस्वरा मताः।
एकैकस्मात् समारभ्य मूर्छनाऽभ्यस्यते बुधैः।८८।
blocks.text: Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha and Ni: these are held to be the seven notes. Beginning from each one in turn, mūrchanā is practised by the wise.

Although we have seated the seven notes on these holes in order so that it is easy to understand, it is not necessary that the hole we have given the place of 'Ma' should always be 'Ma'. If we take the second hole as 'Sa', the third hole can be 'Re'. In ancient times this procedure was called mūrchanā. It would not be inappropriate if we called it the svara sāriṇi procedure. In the making section of this book I have placed all the notes taking ('Ma') as 'Sa', which is the common practice. Here, for the first practice, the first hole is taken as 'Sa', which later on will be taken as 'Pa'. Then again, now and then, for one's own convenience, any one of the above 7 notes may be taken as 'Sa'.
See the svara sāriṇi figure below —

The practitioner should practise 5 of these mūrchanās a hundred times each. And sometimes practise taking all 16 notes up from bottom to top and down from top to bottom in one breath. But do not forget to increase the force of the breath step by step, and then to reduce it on the way back. In this practice keep the speed only such that no note is lost or skipped over and left out. The speed of the fingers will naturally increase little by little, and the breath too will become long. Only when at least two ārohāvaroha (ascents and descents) in one breath are mastered should you consider yourself qualified to play the bānsurī.

blocks.verse:
उपर्युपरि नादेषु फूत्कारो बलवान् भवेत्।
अवरोहे तु नादेषु क्रमसः प्राणन्यूनता।८९।
blocks.text: In each higher sound the blowing should be stronger; and in descending through the sounds there is a gradual lessening of breath.

That is, as the sound climbs higher, more force has to be given to the breath, and when the sound begins to come down, in that descending state weakness comes gradually into the breath. But how much should this more-or-less breath be? In this the guru's (teacher's) contribution will be necessary. Otherwise this judgement can go wrong. In the same way, the second necessary point is that —

blocks.verse:
संयुज्या धस्तनाच्छिद्रा दूर्ध्वच्छिद्रं प्रपूर्यते।
तस्मा दधस्तनं मुक्त्वा तत ऊर्ध्व विमोचयेत्।९०।
blocks.text: The upper hole is completed by joining with the hole below; therefore, having released the lower one, one should then release the upper.

That is, the note from any hole becomes fully true only when at least two holes below that hole are open and the upper hole gets their proper support. Keeping this in mind, when the practitioner opens the first hole from the bottom, then for its completeness he takes support from the lowest hole, which itself always stays open. So if the lower hole has been closed by some chance object, it must certainly be opened. Now, when you lift the second finger, keep the finger lifted before it raised as well. In the same way, while lifting the third finger, keep the first and second fingers open too. But when you lift the first finger of the other hand, that is, the fourth finger, put the first raised finger back on its hole at the same time. Keep that hole closed until the last, that is, the sixth, hole is open. In this way, up to the last hole, all the holes will keep getting the support of their neighbours too, and the bānsurī will not fall from the hand. Then, coming back, as you close three holes from the top, open the lowest finger, and close all the holes in order from the top.

blocks.verse:
आयासस्तु विशेषः स्यात् सप्तकात् सप्तकेऽपरे।
गच्छताम् साधकानां हि तत्पृथक् साध्यताम् मुहुः।९१।
blocks.text: There is special effort for practitioners going from one octave to another; so that should be practised separately, again and again.

That is, after opening all the holes, closing them all at once makes the next note come out as 'Sa' of the second octave. To make this difficulty easy, one should raise and lower five fingers from the top together, again and again. Making the procedure of ārohāvaroha (ascent and descent) on the bānsurī still clearer —

blocks.verse:
यत आरभ्य आरोहस्तस्मिन्नेव समापनम्।
क्रीयतामचरोहोऽपि तेष्वेवाष्टमात्रिकः।९२।
blocks.text: Where the ascent begins, there it should end; let the descent too be made on those same [notes], of eight mātrās (beats).

That is, from whatever note the ascent is made, taking it as 'Sa', end the eighth note, after seven notes, on that same hole. And then, descending from that same note, the eighth count will come back to its earlier place. In this way an ascent of eight mātrās (beats) and a descent of eight mātrās, 16 mātrās in all, will take this form: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni Ṡa, Ṡa Ni Dha Pa Ma Ga Re Sa. By chanting this root mantra of 18 mātrās at least 100 times and at most 1000 times every day, siddhis (accomplishments) are attained. Sometimes, while reciting the 16 mātrās aloud, count them in order with the help of the fingers, as follows —

blocks.verse:
अंगुलीयक एकस्मिन् कूर्याद् भागचतुष्टयम्।
अंगुष्ठाग्रेण गृहणीयात् तांश्च भागान् क्रमेण वै।९३।
blocks.text: On each finger one should make four parts, and take those parts in order with the tip of the thumb.

blocks.verse:
ततः परांगुलीयेषु गणयेत् पूर्ववत् क्रमात्।
तेन षोड़श मात्राः स्यूरंगुलीय चतुष्टयें।९४।
blocks.text: Then on the other fingers one should count in order as before; thus there will be sixteen mātrās (beats) on the four fingers.
That is, if you count by taking each finger as four parts and placing the tip of the thumb on those parts in order, you can easily count up to 16 mātrās (beats).

Just as any flowing river has four directions, so practice too stays alive in four ways: sunanā, cunanā, gunanā and dhunanā — śravaṇa (listening), cayana (choosing), gunana (pondering) and upayoga (use). If you listen to any song or tune with concentration, then pick out from it a few things that matter to you, then sit alone and hum it, and then keep using it at the right time, any practice will keep blossoming and putting out leaves, and will keep flowing along with life. Now some methods of practising the notes with laya (tempo) are presented.

blocks.verse:
अनुध्याय स्वरान् सर्वान् विधिना वादयेन्मुहुः।
गतिं न्यूनाधिकमं कूर्याद् यथाशक्ति शनैः शनैः।९५।
blocks.text: Keeping all the notes in mind, one should play them properly again and again; one should make the speed less or more, gradually, according to one's strength.

While doing the ārohāvaroha (ascent and descent) of the notes, the player should also keep in mind the names of those notes, so that, if asked suddenly, he can quickly play any note and show it. Just as children learning multiplication tables want to repeat from the beginning to answer any question, the same thing happens to those practitioners.
The second suggestion is that if, while playing the ārohāvaroha (ascent and descent), its speed increases, let it increase only so far that the purity of the notes is not spoiled.
The third suggestion is that, while increasing the speed, when some errors appear, correct them at that same speed; then, when you feel unable, reduce that speed little by little.

The fourth point is this: if you take the form of ārohāvaroha (ascent and descent) made in this order — (Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni Ṡa Ṙe Ṡa Ni Dha Pa Ma Ga Re Sa) (ṭa ka ṭa ka ṭa ka ṭa ka ṭa ka ṭa ka ka ṭa ṭa ka) — as a great mantra, and chant it attentively at least a hundred times with mental counting, then along with the fingers, the tongue and the breath, the mind too is trained, and through this practice many kinds of siddhis (accomplishments) are attained. The practitioner can see this for himself through his faith; this secret is not fit to be written.
Now the method of practising the notes with tāla (metric cycle) is presented.

blocks.verse:
अभ्यासस्तालयोगेन स्वराणाम् हि महाफलः।
कालं समं विभाज्याथ स्वराः साध्या मुहुर्मुहुः।९६।
blocks.text: Practice of the notes joined with tāla (metric cycle) bears great fruit; then, dividing time into equal parts, the notes should be practised again and again.

Before practising the notes with tāla (metric cycle), it is necessary to practise the laya (tempo) connected with tāla. The regular movement of anything is called laya. Just as the hand of a clock ticks at regular moments, so if the clap of our hand goes at regular times, we call it laya. Now if we count along with that clap, it will be called a laya of counting equal to the clap.
For example
And if we divide the moment of each clap into two equal parts and say two counts in each clap, the laya (tempo) of the counting will be twice that of the clap, for example —

In the same way, if the moment of the clap is divided into three or four equal parts and as many counts are said, the laya (tempo) of that counting will be called threefold or fourfold. Now if sargam is said in place of the counting, the sargam too will be said to have the same kind of laya. For example —

In the way shown above, while clapping with the hands, one should recite the sargam with the mouth in different layas (tempos). Keep in mind that while doing double [speed] with the mouth, the speed of the hand does not also start to increase. Then, by marking the clap with the foot, the ability to play the sargam on the bānsurī too will develop. Just as a capable witness (a guru) is needed for knowledge of svara, so a witness is needed for knowledge of laya too, one who can turn the incorrect into correct. Now pay attention to the three states of the notes —

blocks.verse:
तत्र वर्णाश्च चत्वारः कथ्यन्ते हि मनीषिभिः।
स्थाय्यारोह्यवरोही च संचारीति यथाक्रमाः।९७।
blocks.text: There, the wise speak of four varṇas (kinds of melodic movement): sthāyī (steady), ārohī (ascending), avarohī (descending) and sañcārī (wandering), in that order.

Just as the four states of stability, rise, decline and busyness give a person many forms and titles, so in the notes, on the basis of the actions of steadiness, climbing, descending and moving about, various groups of notes and tunes arise. A group that is bound to tāla (metric cycle) is called a dhun (tune) or gīt (song). A group that is small and bound only to laya (tempo) we call an alaṅkāra (patterned exercise). Now, there are many texts for the definition of laya and tāla, so after giving a brief introduction to them we will move on to alaṅkāra.

blocks.verse:
लयः स कथ्यते कालः यस्त्वाघातैर्नियन्त्रितः।
मिताघातस्तु तालः स्यात् सून्य विभाजितः।९८।
blocks.text: That time which is regulated by strokes is called laya (tempo); and [laya] with a measured number of strokes, divided by empty [beats], is tāla (metric cycle).

That is, when we regulate the flow of time with regular strokes, that very time is given the name laya (tempo). And when we limit those strokes to a fixed number and divide them with khālī (empty) claps, it is called tāla (metric cycle). Laya is essential in every tāla, but tāla is not necessary in every laya. If laya is the flower, tāla is the garland made of them.

blocks.verse:
मूलाद्यन्तेषु मध्येषु क्रमादन्यस्य योजनम्।
स्पर्ष इत्युच्यते लोके तस्य भेदास्तु द्वादश।९९।
blocks.text: Joining another [note], in order, at the beginning, the end and the middle of the base [note] is called sparśa in the world; it has twelve kinds.

That is, when one note is given prominence and, taking it as the mūla svara (base note), other notes are combined with it in a special way, it begins to take many forms, like conjunct letters. Learned musicians call this action sparśa (touch) or kaṇa (grace note). Mostly the notes that join with a note are its neighbours on either side. If their various forms are counted, there are mainly 12 kinds. Though more than 12 can also be made.

1 - Pūrvādisparśa: if the note before a note is joined at the beginning of the base note, we will call it pūrvādisparśa. For example, the note before 'Ga' is 'Re'; if it is joined at the beginning of the base note, that is, 'Ga', it will be sounded like this: 'Re Ga - -'.

2 - Pūrvamadhyasparśa: if we put that same 'Re' in the middle of 'Ga', then, dividing the time of sounding 'Ga' into four equal parts, 'Re' has to be placed between the first part and the third part, that is, in the second part. Its example will be like this: 'Ga Re Ga -'.

3 - Pūrvāntasparśa: now if 'Re' is joined in the fourth time-division of 'Ga', we will call it pūrvāntasparśa. It can be sounded like this: 'Ga - - Re'. If this is used in movement, this same end-touch begins to seem like the beginning-touch of the next base note.
4 - Parādisparśa: in the same way, the note 'Ma', which follows 'Ga', that is, comes after it, can be joined at the three places in turn.
5 - Paramadhyasparśa: joining [it] at the beginning, the middle and the end of the base note 'Ga',
6 - Parāntasparśa: there can be three kinds, 'MaGa--', 'GaMaGa-' and 'Ga--Ma', whose names are written in order.
7 - Pūrvādyubhayasparśa: if the preceding and the following [notes] are joined to the base note together, there can be conjunct forms such as 'ReMaGa-'.
8 - But if its order is reversed, we will call it parādyubhayasparśa. In sounding, their form will be like this: 'ReMaGa-' and 'MaReGa-'.
9 - Pūrvādi samūlasparśa, and
10 - Parādi samūlasparśa; their example: ReGaMaGa--- MaGaReGa---
Then if these are also begun with the [base] note, two more are formed.
11 - Mūlādyanekasparśa: 'Ga Re Ga Ma Ga-'. These very groups of many joined notes are also called mirkī or murkī.

12 - In this way the glory of the sparśas, taking its endless forms in svaraśāstra (the science of notes), spreads from classical music to folk music. These were the touches of notes on a note; now the touch of śrutis on the notes, which the learned call mīṇḍ (glide), is considered.

blocks.verse:
आरोहस्यावरोहस्य द्वे विधी वर्णिते धिया।
अहि मन्डूक वच्चैव गतिस्तत्र पृथक् पृथक्।१००।
blocks.text: Two methods of ascent and descent are described with thought; the movement in them is, separately, like that of the snake and of the frog.

Wherever there is a question of climbing or descending, two kinds of method are possible: one sliding like a snake, and the other jumping like a frog. On this basis people build steps in their houses for climbing with the feet, and also build a separate slope for taking a bicycle up. If on the bānsurī a long, channel-like hole were made from one hole to another, and one went from the first to the second note by sliding with some smooth metal, this would be called śrutisparśa (touching the śrutis) ascent or descent, because the sounds lying between the first hole, Sa, and the second hole, Re — which we call śrutis — are touched. To master this difficult action, bānsurī players practise not only lifting the fingers but also lacāva (flexing) them. When you raise and set the finger on the hole many times while flexing it, the action of mīṇḍ (glide) will begin to happen. Flex it in whatever direction suits you, so that the hole opens slowly and closes slowly. If one note is far from the other, as in 'Sa Ma', flex the fingers together at the same time, so that the flexing is not broken anywhere.

blocks.verse:
कम्पनम् स्वर एकस्मिन् वैपरीत्यं स्वरद्वये।
स्वरत्रते तु लंघः स्यात् संचारस्तु चतुष्टये।१०१।
blocks.text: On one note there is kampana (shake); on two notes, vaiparītya (reversal); on three notes there is laṅgha (leap); and on four, sañcāra (movement).

Just as in a field of work one person alone can do only a little work, two people together more than that, three together more than that, and four people together accomplish many kinds of tasks — in the same way, making clear which elements grow, when [notes] are used in rāgas, from one note up to four notes, the śloka above has told that as long as any note stays alone, no action other than kampana (shake) can happen in it, as if that note were trembling, frightened of loneliness. But as soon as it meets one other note, many activities begin between the two of them: ādisparśa (touch at the beginning), antasparśa (touch at the end), turning back and forth, and so on. Seen in a worldly way, it seems as if the two have become so absorbed in each other that a third note will have to come to bring them to their senses.

Now when the third also comes and joins, then among those three notes, besides the earlier actions, a new action in the form of laṅghana (leaping) begins, as if the third were now and then making a disturbance between the two notes. After that, when four notes come together, along with the growth of the earlier actions a new action, saṃvāda (dialogue), begins, as if all could become calm and happy. The gradation of qualities grows only up to four notes, so in practice the sargam is what is well known. The actions of different notes among the notes, which come from the mixing of the qualities written above, have been given the name varṇa. So it is from the actions that the varṇa, that is, the class (jāti), is decided.

blocks.verse:
तत्र वर्णाश्च चत्वारः कथ्यन्ते हि मनीषिभिः।
सथाय्यारोद्यवरोही च संचारीति यथा क्रमः।१०२।
blocks.text: There, the wise speak of four varṇas (kinds of melodic movement): sthāyī (steady), ārohī (ascending), avarohī (descending) and sañcārī (wandering), in that order.

In this way these same [actions] have been named the four classes (jātis) of varṇa: sthāyī (steady), ārohī (ascending), avarohī (descending) and sañcārī (wandering). But to make alaṅkāras (patterned exercises), we have to look at those elements of the notes on whose basis alaṅkāras can be made as needed. So, on the basis of the qualities described above, examples of alaṅkāras are presented.
